status.nb: 6 væpnede hendelser meldt de siste sju dagene, 57 prosent færre enn uken før, flest i Caracas, Valencia og Maracaibo.

summary.en: Linares, a former Venezuelan world champion boxer, was detained by US immigration while a gay man was appointed Venezuela's foreign minister, showing internal political shifts. Venezuelan workers launched a 24‑hour strike and protested at Miraflores Palace, and the government used US$12 billion of oil revenue to support the bolívar. A special-forces soldier who bet $400,000 on Maduro's removal made his first court appearance, and a marine died after going overboard in the first US military operation in the Caribbean. Nicolas Maduro is scheduled to stand trial on June 1 2027, and there were 2 battle-related deaths in 2007, according to UCDP.
summary.nb: Linares, en tidligere venezuelansk verdensmester i boksing, ble pågrepet av amerikansk immigrasjonsmyndighet mens en homofil mann ble utnevnt til Venezuelas utenriksminister, noe som viser interne politiske skift. Venezuelanske arbeidere startet en 24‑timers streik og protesterte ved Miraflores-palasset, og regjeringen brukte 12 milliarder dollar av oljeinntektene til å støtte bolívaren. En spesialstyrkesoldat som hadde satset 400 000 dollar på at Maduro skulle fjernes, møtte i første rettsmøte, og en marine døde etter å ha gått overbord i den første amerikanske militæroperasjonen i Karibia. Nicolas Maduro er planlagt til å stå for retten 1. juni 2027, og det var 2 kamprelaterte dødsfall i 2007, ifølge UCDP.

background.title: Crisis in Venezuela
background.extract: An ongoing socioeconomic and political crisis began in Venezuela during the presidencies of Hugo Chávez, Nicolás Maduro as well as Delcy Rodríguez. It has been marked by hyperinflation, starvation, disease, crime, and mortality rates, resulting in massive emigration. Food shortages and hyperinflation have ended, but inflation remains high. It is the worst economic crisis in Venezuela's history and considered by some sources as more severe than the Great Depression in the United States, the 1985–1994 Brazilian economic crisis, or the 2008–2009 hyperinflation in Zimbabwe. In 2019, the Institute of International Finance called it the single largest economic collapse outside of war in 45 years. Writers have compared aspects, such as unemployment and GDP contraction, to Bosnia and Herzegovina after the 1992–95 Bosnian War, and those in Russia, Cuba and Albania following the Revolutions of 1989.
